To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a dual viral infection, in which a flavivirus is administered after an alphavirus, can lead to protection of mice against subsequent challenge with the same flavivirus.

the alphavirus Semlikif Forest (SFV) protects against a challenge with the flavirus Langat (LGV), and that the severity of the pathology seen in mice infected with both viruses is greater than in mice infected with either virus alone.
the alphavirus Semiliki Forest (SFV), which is a neurotropic virus, can be used as a vector to deliver a foreign gene into the central nervous system (CNS) of the mouse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenicity of the alphavirus Semiliki Forest and the flavivirus Langant when inoculated alone and in combination, in the mouse.
the pathogenesis of CNS infections and the role of viral persistence in the pathogenesis and the role of the immune response in protection.
the pathogenesis of dual viral infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the alphavirus Semiliki Forest, when inoculated intraperitonally in the mouse, protected the animals against subsequent challenge with the related flavivirus Langat, and that the protection afforded was due to the presence of anti-glycolipopid antibodies.

the alphavirus Semilki Forest virus protected against a subsequent Langat virus challenge by either persistence of the alphaviral genome or cross-reactive antibodies directed against a common host cell surface glycolipid.
the alphavirus infection of mice was followed by an increased susceptibility to a challenge infection with the flavivirus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alphavirus infection of mice can protect the host against the subsequent challenge with a flavivirus, but this is dependent upon the time interval between the two infections.
a primary infection of mice with an alphavirus, Semliki Forest, can protect against subsequent challenge with a flavivirus, Langat.
the alphavirus interfered with the flavivirus infection, and that this interference was not dependent on the persistence of the alphaviral genome in the host cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
alphaviruses can interfere with flaviviruses and this interference can be beneficial to the host.
alphavirus infection can protect mice against a subsequent challenge of Langat virus and that the degree of protection depends upon the timing of the challenge.
the presence of a virus in a cell can influence the response of the cell to a second virus, and this can have important implications in viral pathogenesis.
